# **Precious metal report** _Gold, silver, platinum and palladium August 2011_ **David Jollie david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** **09 September 2011** #### **New York:** - August was the cruellest month for those trading in the precious metals. All of the major metals suffered from the sort of volatility normally only experienced by rhodium. Gold took the headlines with a move of almost twenty per cent from its lows to its highs and a $200 fall afterwards. Silver and platinum received less media attention but moved nearly as far. The palladium price was comparatively stable but even this saw changes of more than ten per cent during the month. • Central Bank buying of gold continues. The most recent data released concerns July and reveals that both Russia and Colombia were net buyers of metal during that month. Russia’s buying was not at all surprising as it purchased another 4.4 tonnes, taking its reserves to 841 tonnes. Reports suggest that we may see further buying in the weeks ahead. Colombia’s decision was more surprising in that it was the first purchase by that country for more than ten years. The amount of metal bought (2.3 tonnes, taking reserves to a total of 9.1 tonnes) was relatively insignificant but the change in mindset from yet another central bank suggests that reserve diversification through gold is now a mainstream activity in the official sector. • While it might be more reasonable to use a global or gold-specific figure for inflation, almost every calculation of the record price in US Dollar terms in fact uses US CPI as a default. Accepting this, using US CPI figures to adjust for inflation gives us a simple target of $2,468 in today’s money which corresponds to the January 1980 high of $850. Adjusting this for future inflation in the next few months suggests that the increasingly widelymentioned $2,500 per ounce target is in fact not just a round figure but would be a fresh real record price and this number is therefore likely to be at the forefront of some investor’s minds. **_Figure 1_** _: The main theme for investors during August was fear. With the global economy weakening, capital preservation became more important, boosting gold. Silver and platinum mostly traded along with gold but palladium was rather listless._ Macroeconomic factors buffeted the precious metals sector. Unsurprisingly, therefore, gold was the centre of attention with market fundamentals rather less important than attitudes towards risk and the desire to hold or divest gold positions. Silver and platinum showed a close link to the gold price, as can be seen in the figure above but failed to gain from the full safe haven credentials of the yellow metal and consequently underperformed it in comparative terms. Palladium was lonely and unloved by investors and showed little energy of its own with even the platinum:palladium ratio and positive long term fundamentals insufficient to attract buying interest. At the start of August, the US legislature’s overdue agreement to extend the US debt ceiling was announced. With this source of tension removed from the market, gold could have retreated but, instead, the news that one of the agencies had downgraded the USA’s credit rating spurred a rush to gold in its capacity as a “safe haven” against risk. Gold climbed $150 in a week, further aided by a Swiss National Bank decision to inject liquidity into its currency in an attempt to make it less attractive to speculators. Weak economic data depressed the other precious metals, all of which are

more sensitive to industrial demand than gold. 

On the 8<sup>th</sup> of August, gold moved above platinum, forcing some investors into action to trade this price ratio. Historically, platinum has rarely traded below gold and, whatever the rationale, trading this ratio has generally been profitable. It was not surprising therefore when platinum started to follow gold higher as it continued upwards, aided by a challenging industrial relations climate within the South African mining industry. For the rest of the month, platinum largely ignored the impact of further negative economic developments and accompanied gold instead. Silver essentially plotted the same course as platinum and gold from here on in, with its precious character outweighing the industrial aspect of its behaviour. Palladium slowly gained ground but showed little link to the other metals. 

Fresh concerns over European sovereign debt – French this time – drove gold over $1,800 for the first time ever on the 11<sup>th</sup> of August. With the gold price apparently spiralling out of control, margins were increased on the Shanghai Gold Exchange and on COMEX that day, driving gold back $50 below its peak with silver and platinum weakening too.

Interestingly, the US Federal Reserve’s comments that interest rates would remain low into 2013 drove a greater acceptance of risk and a small sell-off of gold, suggesting that QE3, should it happen, might be less positive for gold than for some other assets. 

Later, weak European economic data restarted gold’s move higher. Gold powered to a new record $1,910 and above as stock markets tumbled due to these woes. Platinum and silver followed. However, the market was over-extended at this point and further margin increases on the same two exchanges on the 25<sup>th</sup> drove strong selling, forcing gold roughly $200 lower in only two days. Platinum and silver followed. Comments by some people that this marked the end for the “gold bubble” seem to have been rather premature, however, with gold recovering much of the recently-lost ground in moving to end the month at $1,825, taking its new friends along for the journey. 

### **Quantitative easing – QE3** 

The QE3 debate has started much as the QE2 debate started in Q3 2010 following the US Federal Reserve’s annual Jackson Hole meeting. The background for this speculation is, as it was last year, a proliferation of weak economic data. Worryingly, though, on this occasion, it is not just the USA that is suffering. Consumer confidence is weak throughout much of Europe and North America with inflation outpacing both interest rates and pay awards and eroding consumers’ purchasing power. Economic growth in China and some of the other developing nations is also weakening. Given that this has been one of the most important factors in supporting the global economy, this has led the market to worry about

**_Figure 2_** _: Public interest in QE3 is increasing, suggesting that a weakening economy is expected to drive the world’s central banks back into quantitative easing._ However, America remains the focus for most investors. With the Federal Reserve expressing its view that unemployment remains stubbornly high, the market has come to the realisation that something has to be done. A consensus seems to be developing that this will be quantitative easing, so-called QE3. Arguments abound as to whether QE and QE2 were successful or not. However, with other approaches such as the provision of tax rebates or the writing off of a portion of home loans taking longer to affect the economy, QE3 may appear to be a more attractive option. The environment is, though, perhaps not as welcoming for QE3 as it was for QE2: the political debate within the USA has turned against quantitative easing, making it more challenging to restart this process. It is also not clear that reducing bond yields and interest rates is the key to stimulating lending and kick-starting the economy: with unemployment stubbornly high, economic output weak and many home-owners still “under water”, there seems little reason to borrow money to use for normal economic purposes. Additionally, there are signs of nascent inflation in many countries, suggesting that greater care must be taken in timing the withdrawal of any stimulus. 4 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 September 2011** Nonetheless, while there are many other actions that could be taken in order to stimulate the economy, we expect that some degree of quantitative easing will occur in the USA. It is likely to be smaller than the previous rounds, it may be targeted differently and it may go by a different name but we expect to see QE3 arrive at some point later this year or early next year. There may be more effective actions that could be taken (for instance repurchasing distressed stock in the housing market and demolishing it) but the immediacy of quantitative easing and the fact that it is within the control of the Federal Reserve are likely to make QE an attractive option. There is also increasing chatter over the prospects for launching further QE in the UK. We would not be surprised to see this happen and feel it should add to the upwards pressure on precious metals prices. In terms of price expectations, we see QE3 as having a similar, but perhaps smaller, impact to that of QE2. The prices of silver and palladium both started to move higher as speculation that QE2 would take place increased in Q3 2010 (platinum and gold benefited too but to a lesser extent). As further QE becomes more likely, a range of asset prices should start to rise, including the precious metals. As a result, we feel that further economic weakness which makes QE more palatable in the short term should be beneficial for the prices of all of the precious metals to some degree. 5 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 September 2011** ### **The death of safe havens** Just as the demise of Bear Stearns made many investors more aware of the distinctions between banks in terms of their creditworthiness, the continued struggles of the global economy have reminded people of the value of safe havens. Gold has benefited as the “safest” of “safe havens”. While its value may ebb and flow, in the extreme case of the end of civilised society, enough people believe that a gold coin will retain some value. However, assuming that society does not break down, there is a wider range of possible “safe havens” in which to invest. Historically, there are relatively few assets which are viewed as safe in times of market stress. These would normally include gold, and to a lesser extent silver, a few currencies including the Swiss Franc and the Dollar and a range of bonds of the major nations, principally including Germany, Japan and the USA. Many of these have performed relatively well during the most recent phase of the economic crisis in their role of capital preservation (with the US Dollar the main exception). However, as the correlations between different asset classes have increased, the ideal “safe haven” investment has become more difficult to find. Historically, the shares of the gold miners have been used as a proxy for the gold price and therefore a safe haven. However, over recent months as the global economy has started to wilt, gold has out

performed these shares. There are a number of possible causes for this divergence (including cost control, gearing and forecasts of future price declines) but we believe that this primarily reflects an unselective view of all equities as risky assets and the physical metal as a place of safety. 6 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 September 2011** The recent downgrading of the US credit rating (at the start of August) means that what would typically be viewed as a risk-free asset cannot now be viewed in quite the same way. The travails of many of the Eurozone governments over debt issues have placed question marks over the health of the Euro too. German bonds remain attractive compared to other European bonds but the uncertain future for the Euro makes these an interesting choice as a safe haven. Nonetheless, in recent weeks as concern over global growth has intensified, even these imperfect “safeish havens” have attracted capital inflows with yields falling substantially. The Swiss Franc saw similar “benefits” as a safe haven throughout the first half of 2011. In fact, it looked like a slightly more attractive version of gold, with an interest rate and a lower haircut when used as collateral. In Swiss Franc terms, gold barely moved throughout that period. However, at the start of August, the Swiss National Bank announced its first plan to flood the market with liquidity. This started to make it clear to investors that the Franc is just like any other currency in that it can be created at will. Unsurprisingly, it was sold off with XAUCHF rising from 1,300 to 1,500 demonstrating a clear preference for gold over this new “slightly safe haven” of the CHF. Looking at the 6th September Swiss announcement that it intended to buy “unlimited quantities” of foreign currency in order to peg their currency to the Euro, the jump of over 100 in XAUCHF merely reinforces the fact that safe havens are fewer in number than they were before. With plenty of economic turbulence to come in the next few months, the need for capital preservation seems unlikely to diminish quickly and the gold price seems set to appreciate as the best of a bad set of choices for this role.

**_Figure 7_** _: The Swiss Franc had already ceased to be an effective safe haven before the Swiss National Bank announced its plans to peg its currency to the Euro._ 7 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 September 2011** ## **Gold** How best to describe the movements of the gold price during August? A rapid climb from $1,610 to a closing $1,825, an increase of 13.4 per cent? A continuation of a ten year-long bull run? The first stages of a bubble? A series of new all-time nominal highs recorded up to $1,912 or a $200 fall from the highs in just two days which taught investors a valuable lesson? All of these and more would give an accurate description of at least one facet of gold’s price performance throughout the month. To give some perspective, gold had traded around the $1,500-$1,550 level for most of the months of May and June, ending June weakly with the cessation of the second round of US quantitative easing (QE2) making investors more wary than they had previously been. Since that point, the gold price has been rising for much of the time, reaching $1,615, itself a nominal record price, at the end of July and a peak of $1,912 on the 23rd of August. **_Figure 8_** _: Gold exceeded $1,900 for the first time ever in August 2011._ The driving forces for this upwards movement in the price appear to have been simple and numerous. As has been the case throughout this year, consumers, whether European, Chinese or Indian have continued to buy gold as an investment and a hedge against risk. The macroeconomic environment continued to disappoint too: slowing growth in North America was accompanied by a worsening outlook for the Chinese economy. July saw the price driven still higher by concerns that a dysfunctional US government might not extend its debt ceiling in time to avoid defaulting on some of its obligations. However, as soon as this issue was solved, other worries took its place: a sign of a bullish market. The downgrade of the US credit rating damaged the attractiveness of the US Dollar as a home for nervous capital. The first stage of intervention by the Swiss National Bank at the start of August weakened the Franc and removed another safe haven, adding to the attraction of gold. A general lack of belief in the ability or desire of European leaders to address Eurozone debt issues increased risk aversion and drove gold onward. And, to cap this all, the first signs of renewed debate on the advisability of launching QE3 in A

merica (and other QE elsewhere in the world) started to emerge in late August. 

Throughout almost all of this period the gold price rose. However, the ride upwards was not smooth: gold tumbled from $1,815 on the 11<sup>th</sup> to $1,725 on the 12<sup>th</sup> as both the Shanghai Gold Exchange and COMEX increased margin requirements on their contracts. The respite was only temporary and, with the price moving over $1,900 on the 22<sup>nd</sup> , the imposition of yet higher margins on both exchanges drove some panicked selling which ended with the price crashing to $1,705 just two days later. The price recovered to $1,820 by the end of the month, keeping the bullish trend intact and leaving one to wonder just where gold would have been at that point without the margin changes.

### **Futures margins** 

Margins on the various gold contracts on the Shanghai Gold Exchange were raised twice during August as speculative interest overheated in the run up to new all-time record prices. Margins were raised to 11 per cent on all the gold contracts at the close on the 11<sup>th</sup> of August and to 12 per cent at the end of trading on the 25<sup>th</sup> of August in an attempt to cool market interest. 

Likewise, margins were raised on gold contracts on COMEX on the 11<sup>th</sup> and 25<sup>th</sup> . The two major falls in the gold price during the month of August appear to have been triggered by these margin increases which reduced the maximum leverage available on a futures position, in effect making it more expensive to hold. This should act as a reminder to investors that the futures exchanges and regulators will not necessarily stand by and simply watch prices accelerate upwards. However, given that these downwards movements were artificially triggered (i.e. not initially caused by changes in investor or consumer attitude or behaviour) this suggests that bullish sentiment persists. 

### **Official sector activity** 

Central Bank buying of gold continues. The most recent data released concerns July and reveals that both Russia and Colombia were net buyers of metal during that month. Russia’s buying was not at all surprising as it purchased another 4.4 tonnes from domestic production, taking its reserves to 841 tonnes. Reports suggest that we may see further buying in the weeks ahead. Colombia’s decision was more surprising in that it was the first purchase by that country for more than ten years. The amount of metal bought (2.3 tonnes, taking reserves to a total of 9.1 tonnes) was relatively insignificant but the change in mindset from yet another central bank suggests that reserve diversification through gold is now a mainstream activity in the official sector. 

Additionally, a widely circulated report seems to suggest that China is buying gold for its reserves. Unfortunately, the information in the report itself dates from the first half of

2009, _suggesting that it may not be all that current_ . Nonetheless, we fully understand and agree with the rationale for why China should be purchasing gold. The lack of updated data on Chinese official sector gold holdings makes any comments on this subject speculative by their very nature. However, although we discount this report, we would be surprised if China is not buying gold and we believe that this is bullish for the gold price both in the short term and whenever such buying is eventually revealed publicly. Interestingly, though, two countries apparently reduced their holdings of gold during the month of July. This selling has been relatively rare in recent months but, nonetheless, Kazakhstan sold 3.1 tonnes of gold while Tajikistan disposed of 1.2 tonnes of gold. More importantly, despite speculation over the matter, no significant selling of gold was reported by any European bank despite the ongoing debt crisis there. Elsewhere, the Venezuelan Government announced its plans to nationalise the local gold industry. Venezuela is a relatively small producer of gold from either the formal or informal mining sector but this type of government intervention is at least marginally bullish for gold as nationalisation tends to have a negative impact on mine output. The Government has also decided to repatriate its gold reserves from overseas vaults in case any attempts are made to seize its assets. Its total metal holdings are 365.8 tonnes, which is not insignificant. However, we do not expect this individual action to have any significant impact on the gold market. ### **US coin sales and ETF investment** Sales of gold coins by the US Mint climbed from between 60,000 and 65,000 ounces in each of June and July to 112,000 ounces in August. This is the highest August figure 9 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 September 2011** since 1999 and could reflect heightened fears over the economic situation. However, monthly sales are somewhat “lumpy” and we feel it is more informative to focus on rolling six month or cumulative year-to-date sales. These sales are running close to but below the level of 2010 and 2009 although they are substantially higher than in previous years, illustrating investors' focus on risk aversion following the global economic crisis (or the first phase of the global economic crisis for the pessimists amongst us). **_Figure 12_** _: ....but they do look similar to patterns of investment in gold on COMEX._ ### **Real and nominal record prices and targets** During August, gold recorded a series of all-time nominal record prices as it has repeatedly done throughout the past year. With the price in uncharted territory, there are relatively few upside targets still available for investors. Of course, the big round figure numbers remain as possible attractors of interest: $2,000 per ounce, a figure that might have seemed outlandish only a few years ago seems to be the first major target and numerous market commentators have started to point out longer term targets of anywhere from $2,500 to $5,000. Setting aside any arguments of whether this overt and extreme bullishness is justified and whether gold is in a bubble, we think it is interesting to view the current prices in real rather than nominal terms. Calculating the real (inflation-adjusted) record price of gold is not a trivial exercise. It is well-known that the constituent parts of most consumer price indices (CPI) are changed periodically and that some costs such as housing are excluded. As a result, long run CPI 11 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Monthly Precious Metal Report** **09 September 2011** data is somewhat unreliable as a guide to real inflation. It may be possible to use other measures such as purchasing power to give a better guide to what real inflation is. The second, and probably more important point, is that since gold is priced in US Dollars for most consumers, US inflation data is commonly used for this calculation. As a recent article by Fergal O’Connor and Brian Lucey of Trinity College Dublin (http://www.lbma.org.uk/ assets/The_Real_Price_of_Gold.pdf) questions, why, if gold is a currency, should we use an inflation rate for another currency in determining its real, inflation-adjusted level. Unfortunately, they caution that no gold-specific inflation figures exist to allow us to find a more appropriate inflation rate for our calculation. Thus, while it might be more reasonable to use a global or gold-specific figure for inflation, almost every calculation of the record price in US Dollar terms in fact uses US CPI as a default. Accepting this and using US CPI figures to adjust for inflation gives us a simple target of $2,468 in today’s money which corresponds to the January 1980 high of $850. Adjusting this for future inflation in the next few months suggests that the $2,500 per ounce figure mentioned above is in fact not just a round figure but would also be a fresh real record price and this target is therefore likely to be at the forefront of some investor’s minds. (For interest, the inflation-adjusted record highs for the other precious metals are: $144 for silver, $2,408 for platinu

m and $1,411 for palladium.) With gold at record prices in nominal terms (and sometimes in inflation-adjusted terms) in many other currencies, there are few other meaningful targets to chase except for the traditional round figures. However, we note that plenty of targets remain in one currency: the recent 2011 high in the Japanese gold price was 145,752 Yen per ounce (or 4,686 Yen per g) compared to the 1980 high of 204,850 Yen per ounce (or (6,586 Yen per g) in nominal terms… ### **Investor attitudes to gold** Gold’s rising investment profile was brought into focus in a recent Gallup poll. This has been carried out annually in the USA since 2002, asking what Americans see as the best long term investment. Prior to 2010, gold was not included as a possible answer. On this occasion, however, fully 34 per cent of respondents listed gold as their preferred asset in answer to this question. Remarkably, considering gold’s status as a “barbarous relic”, over a quarter of 18-29 year-olds surveyed also thought gold was the best long term investment available at the moment. Other perspectives on investor attitudes can be seen elsewhere. Fleet car and commercial vehicle sales seem to be relatively robust as companies are forced to replace units whose retirement was delayed by the global economic crisis. In the UK, there was finally some positive news as sales of new cars rose in August for the first time in more than a year. However, the year-to-date performance is much weaker, showing a year-on-year decline of 6.1 per cent (a decrease of roughly 80,000 cars and equivalent to roughly 8-10,000 ounces of platinum group metals). The picture for platinum demand is, though, markedly more positive. Most commercial vehicles s

old are dieselpowered and therefore use catalytic aftertreatment which uses platinum (often alongside palladium). Due to their fuel efficiency and tax advantages, fleet car sales are also disproportionately skewed in favour of diesel cars over gasoline variants. Overall, therefore, although January-August sales of gasoline cars fell by 120,000 units, diesel car sales actually increased by almost 40,000 cars or 6.5 per cent, a positive for platinum. 

For the optimist, it was worth noting that Spanish car sales increased 5.9 per cent yearon-year in August. However, August 2010 saw the weakest sales for 20 years, so this does not suggest a healthy economy. Indeed, the more representative figures is the decrease in sales of 22 per cent for the first eight months of the year after fourteen consecutive monthly falls. Astonishingly, 2011 sales are running at barely half of pre-crisis levels. With the Spanish economy struggling, weak sales can be expected for the rest of 2011 and into 2012. 

Germany remains the healthiest car market within Europe, with sales rising 11 per cent for the year-to-date and an impressive 18 per cent in August itself. Production within Germany and vehicle exports from Germany both increased by 8 per cent in the first eight months of the year compared to a year earlier. 

Looking outside Europe, A recent article in the China Daily focused on the challenges facing producers of diesel vehicles in China. Hawtai Motors has chosen to focus on the diesel sector since 2000 but its sales had only reached an annual 16,000 units by the start of this year. Despite their mixed reputation, a greater market penetration of diesel vehicles would allow countries like China to reduce the average carbon dioxide emissions of their vehicle fleet. However, Chinese imports of diesel are somewhat limited and, with huge amounts of diesel being used by the construction industry, there are occasionally shortages of fuel available to members of the public. Additionally, diesel fuel is more expensive than gasoline, so fuel efficiency improvements do not translate directly to cost savings, unlike in many countries within Europe. Progress will be slow. 

However, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, new emissions rules will soon be introduced on smaller diesel vehicles (below 3.5 tonnes unladen weight, meaning cars and small trucks only). These rules, which were initially set to be introduced in 2010, should force the use of relatively low-loaded platinum or platinum/

### **Southern Africa watch** 

In our July monthly report, we commented on the wage negotiations then ongoing in the South African mining sector. In the platinum industry, these typically take place every two years and discussions can be fractious, providing some support for the price of this metal. So far this year, however, they have been relatively quiet. Anglo American Platinum reached agreement with the National Union of Miners in early September without any strike action occurring. There was a short-lived strike at ARM and Norilsk Nickel’s Nkomati joint venture but there have been few other strikes as yet across the industry. 

Although discussions continue at a number of producers and more strikes may yet occur, the likelihood of widespread disruption appears to be receding and this source of support for the platinum price should weaken. Of longer term relevance, the wage deals agreed so far have tended to be for annual increases approaching ten per cent. This is inflationary and can only lead to higher platinum production costs and prices in the future. 

We also reported on the growing tide of nationalism throughout the mining industry with governments trying to extract more money from this sector at a time of high commodity prices. In mid-August, the Zimbabwean Government rejected all of the indigenisation proposals it had received from majority foreign-owned mining companies operating within Zimbabwe, including the three active platinum mines. All of the companies concerned were given fourteen days to resubmit proposals, taking them up to the end of August. There is little public information available on this issue relating to Anglo American Platinum’s Unki mine. However, the minister responsible did comment on the other two mines, stating that he believed that agreement could be reached on Mimosa. 

On Zimplats (Ngezi), he was much less positive, suggesting that its operating licence could be cancelled. Few political issues in Zimbabwe are ever entirely clear and we do not expect this matter to be clarified quickly. We do expect an agreement to be reached, meaning that there should be little impact on platinum group metal output. However, this process and confusion have been negative for investment within Zimbabwe and therefore positive for the metal prices. We will report on this issue further as more information emerges.

omic output slowing and even previously quickly-growing economies such as Brazil and China beginning to struggle, car sales and output are set to disappoint this year, with palladium and rhodium demand being lower than had initially been expected. Demand will, nonetheless, be higher than in 2010 as the market is still growing. 

In Japan, vehicle output has recovered well from the earthquake, tsunami and nuclear accident. It has not yet returned to normal but should do so in September. H1 2011 output was 3.43 million units, 1.4 million lower than a year earlier due to the impact of the disaster. According to Toyota, it now plans to produce and sell 2.79 million cars in Japan during the calendar year (in addition to units produced by its Hino and Daihatsu subsidiaries). This is 310,000 units lower than was forecast at the start of the year. However, it is some 140,000 units higher than was forecast during June, demonstrating that the supply chain has recovered more quickly than was initially expected. It is worth noting that the original production target for the year was already lower than the 2010 figure, reflecting concern over weak domestic demand and the impact of a strong Yen. At Nissan, first half Japanese production decreased by 18 per cent year-on-year but output in June was, remarkably, higher than a year earlier and almost back to normal levels. Honda’s recovery to normal production levels within Japan should be complete in Q3 too. 

The North American market is still rather sickly. August sales were broadly acceptable but the annualised running rate is now 12.1 million units, substantially weaker than the 13 million figure at the start of the year. With many indicators (such as the Purchasing Manager Indices) pointing to a slower US economy in the second half of the year, there must be some prospect of sales falling below this figure. On a more positive note, oil prices have fallen and may mitigate some of the consumer preference that has developed for smaller, cheaper to operate cars which use less palladium and rhodium in their catalysts. Additionally, incentives available to purchasers of new cars fell by 6.1 per cent in August to $2,615 per vehicle as the US automakers made the most of a lack of competition from their Japanese competitors. It seems likely that, as Japanese models become more widely available, competition will increase in this marketplace and incentives will increase once again. This should attract additional consumers and we are therefore a little more positive than the consensus forecast for the outlook for the remainder of this year. 

Sales are, though, still expected to remain relatively weak as the US struggles to avoid a double dip recession. Falling consumer confidence, higher fuel prices and lower incentives have all taken their toll. Fleet sales weakened throughout the second quarter and are now running level with year earlier figures, having been significantly ahead of Q1 2010 in the first quarter of this

year. We take this as a negative for automotive palladium demand and a worrying signal of worsening business confidence. However, high second hand vehicle prices have driven some consumers to purchase new rather than used vehicles, providing some additional sales. 

Finally, in China, The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers now expects vehicle sales to rise by roughly 5 per cent this year. Our expectation is that the market will outperform this target as the Chinese Government intervenes to keep the economy growing quickly. July passenger vehicle sales were 1.01 million units, lower than the June figure due to normal seasonal factors but almost 7 per cent more than in July 2010. There are already signs that Chinese automotive demand could accelerate in H2. China continues to add vehicles to the list of those eligible for its environmental subsidies. It also revealed a plan to pay consumers up to 18,000 RMB (roughly US$2,750) if they scrap a car that is between 6 and 15 years old and purchase a new car in 2011. 

Despite differential taxation in favour of smaller cars, sales of larger sports utility vehicles continue to outpace growth in the rest of this market, with 20 per cent more sold in July 2011 than in July 2010. Forecasts are for SUV sales to approach US levels by the end of the decade. Overall, vehicle sizes and engine sizes are increasing, leading to higher metal loadings within China.
